title: Set phrases worth knowing whole
intro: Fixed expressions that no amount of word-by-word knowledge will give you. Learn each as a single unit, the way you learned the greetings in unit 5.

entries.note: The commonest way to express obligation, ahead of deber. hay que is the impersonal version: one must.
The everyday future. Spanish has a proper future tense but this outnumbers it in speech.

ex.en: I'm going to call her tomorrow.

entries.note: See unit 40. acabo de comer, I've just eaten.
See unit 1. Where English adds again, Spanish uses a verb.

ex.en: He asked the same thing again.
I was about to call you.

entries.note: See unit 24. Nothing to do with realizar.

ex.es: No se dio cuenta del error.

entries.note: See unit 20. The natural way to say you feel like doing something.

entries.en: not to matter, to make no difference
entries.note: Built like gustar. me da igual is I don't mind either way.

ex.en: I don't mind where we eat.

ex.es: Dura por lo menos dos horas.
ex.en: It lasts at least two hours.

ex.es: Son más o menos veinte minutos.

entries.note: Unlike quizá it takes the indicative: a lo mejor viene.

ex.es: A lo mejor llueve por la tarde.

entries.note: ¿En serio? is the everyday really? tomar en serio is to take seriously.

ex.en: Did he really say that to you?

entries.note: Short for no tengo ni idea.
otra vez is commoner in speech. See volver a above for the verb version.
¡Qué bonito! ¡Qué lástima! ¡Qué calor! The commonest exclamation pattern in the language.

entries.en: what a shame, what a pity
entries.note: In Colombia ¡qué pena! also means sorry or how embarrassing.

ex.en: What a shame you couldn't come!

entries.en: it doesn't matter; it's fine, no harm done
entries.note: no pasa nada is the standard reassurance after an apology.

ex.en: It doesn't matter, we'll do it later.
Take an umbrella just in case.

entries.note: The standard encouragement to a learner, and true of this book.
